item.title: Hundreds of thousands more to pay tax on savings, NOS says
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands more to pay tax on savings, NOS says

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Hundreds of thousands more people in the Netherlands are set to pay tax on their savings and investments from 2028 under a revised plan for box 3, the tax on wealth, according to leaked details of the cabinet’s deliberations with opposition parties.

Box 3 covers savings, shares, crypto and second homes, and around 2.5 million people currently pay it, according to broadcaster NOS. At present the tax rate is 36% on an assumed return on those assets, with a tax-free allowance of €59,357 per person.

Under a new law on box 3 rules approved by MPs in February, people were to pay tax on unrealised returns on most assets every year, meaning they would pay tax on increased asset values regardless of whether they have sold the assets and made any money.

This plan is set to be dropped for shares, according to NOS, and people will only pay tax on gains from shares once they sell them. This was a demand by right-wing parties such as far-right JA21.

Initially, the new system was to allow a tax-free return of €1,800 per person a year. That has reportedly been cut to €1,000, helping offset the losses anticipated by moving to a realised gains system.

Businesses affected 

People who run their own private limited company (bv) will also be affected. The amount they can borrow from their own company on favourable tax terms is set to fall from €500,000 to €100,000. The rules on borrowing from a company to buy a home will stay the same.

At the same time, tax on profits that owners pay out to themselves will be cut for 4 years. The aim is to encourage them to take money out of the company, which would bring in extra tax revenue in the short term.

The measures are expected to raise almost €500 million more than needed. The cabinet wants to use that to cut income tax, but has not yet said how.

Welfare cuts dropped

The leaked plans also confirm that planned cuts to social security are off the table, as left-wing Pro and pan-European party Volt said this week. Hans Spekman, chairman of the country’s largest trade union FNV, said on Monday evening that the unions would return to talks with the cabinet if the cuts were scrapped. Political sources told NOS that could happen as soon as next week.

JA21 said part of the funding for the box 3 changes was “unacceptable” because it hits small investors. Jan Struijs, parliamentary leader of pensioners’ party 50PLUS, said he wanted a “stress test” to show what the plans would mean for police officers, nurses and pensioners.

Finance minister Eelco Heinenis expected to set out the details in a letter to parliament ahead of this week’s budget debate. The minority cabinet needs opposition votes to get its budget through both houses of parliament.

item.title: Netherlands “blocked” Machado’s efforts to return to Venezuela
item.description:
Netherlands “blocked” Machado’s efforts to return to Venezuela

September 29, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch government has been accused of blocking the return of Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to her home country after she was twice unable to fly from Curaçao and Aruba.

Two flights were cancelled at short notice last Tuesday because of administrative “technicalities” that arose after she had booked to travel, according to a Spanish journalist who was embedded with her to document the trip.

The Nobel peace prize winner had hoped to slip into Venezuela while the country’s interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, was in New York for the United Nations general assembly last week.

Officially the Netherlands supports Machado’s return to Venezuela so that free democratic elections can be held, something that has not happened since former president Nicolas Maduro was captured by US forces in January and replaced by Rodriguez, who was vice-president in Maduro’s regime.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said at his weekly press conference on Friday: “If Venezuela is serious about working towards a future where relations with the Netherlands and Europe are normalised, one of our conditions is that progress is made towards free and fair elections.

“Those elections are only possible if opposition leaders can participate in them.”

Trump oil deal

But behind the scenes, the Trump administration appears to be concerned that Machado’s return could destabilise the interim regime, which has struck a deal with Washington giving the US control of 65 billion barrels of crude oil reserves.

Leiden university professor Wouter Veenendaal, who specialises in relations between the nations in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, told Dutch News: “I can’t prove it, but it sounds to me like The Hague has been put under pressure by the Americans.

“Although the Americans formally take a positive view of Machado, her arrival is seen as potentially threatening the relative stability that they’ve been able to create with the interim president.”

Machado has made seven attempts to reach Venezuela by land, sea and air in recent months, including twice from Curaçao and once from Aruba, but every time her efforts have been thwarted by administrative or technical problems.

Last Tuesday a ferry trip from Panama City, where she is currently living, was cancelled hours before the boat was due to leave port after the operator claimed to have discovered a serious defect with the engine.

Paperwork problem

David Alandete, a journalist with the Spanish newspaper ABC who was invited to travel with Machado, said it was clear that the Dutch government, which controls the Caribbean islands’ foreign policy, “had a hand in preventing Machado from reaching Aruba, Curaçao or Bonaire”.

“This was not simply a paperwork problem. A European government was part of the chain of decisions that kept her from moving closer to Venezuela,” he wrote on social media site X.

Is María Corina Machado a prisoner in Panama? Why has the Nobel Peace Prize winner been prevented from returning to her own country seven times? I have the facts firsthand from Panama. I was with her team this weekend and witnessed the latest attempts—and the refusals. The full… pic.twitter.com/Jk4iBuop3m

— David Alandete (@alandete) September 23, 2026

“Clearly there is something that is preventing Maria Corina Machado from returning,” Alandete said. “She has tried to enter and she’s been unable to do it.”

Jetten would neither confirm nor deny at his press conference whether the Netherlands was behind the decision to cancel Machado’s flights.

“It’s not in the interests of the co-operation we have with the [Venezuelan] opposition and the responsibility we feel for its members to say any more about it,” he said.

Caribbean journalists who asked Eric van der Burg, junior minister for kingdom relations, about the episode last week were redirected to the foreign affairs ministry in The Hague. “I can say extremely little about it,” he said, according to the Antilliaans Dagblad.

Jetten also hinted that he had been unable to persuade Rodriguez to guarantee Machado’s safe return to her country when he spoke to the interim president at the UN last week.

“It’s important that Machado and others are able to travel freely to Venezuela, and that’s why I brought it to the interim president’s attention.”

Veenendaal said the episode was typical of the way the Dutch govern Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao, which are semi-autonomous nations within the kingdom, and the “democratic deficit” in their administration.

Colonial history

The islands are represented by Van der Burg at the cabinet table in The Hague, but have no say in which issues are raised. Their parliaments have no powers to question cabinet ministers about foreign policy or defence.

“A lot of decisions are taken over their heads, which is a sensitive point given the colonial history,” Veenendaal said.

“In the past the Americans have exerted a lot of pressure on The Hague behind the scenes, for example to prevent the islands becoming independent, but also because they have air bases on the islands so that they can keep an eye on Venezuela.”

“I can see Jetten’s government thinking: ‘choose your battles’. Let the Americans get their way here so that the Americans give them an easier ride on other issues such as the International Criminal Court or Ukraine.”

item.title: Five arrested after luggage left unattended at railway stations
item.description:
Five arrested after luggage left unattended at railway stations

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Five people have been arrested after four railway stations had to be partly evacuated on Tuesday morning when luggage was left unattended.

Haarlem station and surrounding buildings were closed and cleared after two stray bags were reported at around 10.15am. Some trains were unable to stop at the station.

Luggage was also left standing in Rotterdam, Utrecht and Dordrecht. Police said there was no evidence that the incidents were linked, but they described the situation as “highly unusual”.

Three people were arrested at Haarlem station, while two others were detained at Utrecht Centraal after camera footage showed them acting suspiciously just before they dumped the bags.

In Rotterdam a pedestrian tunnel was evacuated while police checked two abandoned suitcases for possible explosives.

A woman in Rotterdam later came forward to say she had left the bags while she went into the city centre. She was not arrested.

Spokesman Jan Martijn Stout told NOS the incidents appeared to be unconnected, but the suspects were be questioned about why they had left the bags behind.

“Their role is being investigated because it was a significant disruption to public order,” he said.

item.title: Netherlands demands hundreds of billions in EU budget cuts
item.description:
Netherlands demands hundreds of billions in EU budget cuts

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch government has co-signed a letter to the EU presidency demanding the bloc’s next budget, which is set every seven years, be dramatically scaled back.

Prime minister Rob Jetten’s minority coalition is one of six so-called “frugal” governments, whose countries pay more into the EU budget than they get back.

The European Commission has proposed an almost €2 trillion budget for the 2028-2034 period, which governs spending on everything from agriculture to defence and funding for poorer regions.

Along with Germany, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, and Finland, the Netherlands is now pressing for a cut of several hundred billion euros from the proposals.

The letter, which has not been made public but has been seen by major news outlets, states: “Our six countries alone finance almost 40% of all Member States’ contributions. While net contributors as a whole are in the minority, they shoulder around three-quarters of the total financing burden.”

An almost €2 trillion budget would represent a 60% nominal increase in the size of the current budget, which, they argue, is “simply not realistic.”

Divisions
There are 17 other countries, including Spain and Italy, who are insisting on protections for impoverished regions and struggling sectors like agriculture, and want the overall budget raised above €2 trillion.

The Commission has also suggested creating new EU-wide taxes, including a levy on large companies and a tobacco excise duty, to raise capital and ease the burden on countries like the Netherlands. In June, the Cypriot presidency proposed a 2% cut to the Commission’s plan, which the six considered far too small.

Negotiators want to get a deal done by the end of the year, before elections in France, Italy, Spain and Poland complicate the talks. All 27 member states must agree to the budget.

But according to the Financial Times, a diplomat from one of the six countries said there would be no deal this year unless the budget was cut by hundreds of billions of euros.

Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, is due to present a new compromise text in the coming days, ahead of a summit of EU leaders on October 15 and 16. European Council president António Costa will meet Jetten in the Netherlands on October 9 to discuss the budget.

Jetten’s shift
The letter marks a U-turn for Jetten, whose D66 party went into the 2025 election calling for a European budget twice its current size, financed by new EU-level taxes. The same manifesto proposed €750 to €800 billion a year in extra European investment, paid for with joint borrowing.

In office with his minority coalition, Jetten has taken a different line. At an informal EU summit in Cyprus in April, he rejected the €2 trillion proposal, telling reporters the Dutch contribution would “explode” under the plan, according to De Telegraaf. In June he told NOS the Commission’s proposal was “simply not good enough”.

A big part of the reason is money – at the moment, the Netherlands gets a discount on its EU bill. Brussels wants to end that discount, which would cost the Dutch around €2 billion more a year. In total, the plans would add up to €5.4 billion a year to what the Netherlands pays the EU, according to the Court of Audit, the government’s spending watchdog.

item.title: Five things every first-time buyer in the Netherlands must know
item.description:
Partner content

Five things every first-time buyer in the Netherlands must know

September 29, 2026

Buying your first home is one of the biggest financial decisions most people make in their lives. And as an international in the Netherlands, it’s likely that the process, language and unwritten rules are all different from what you might expect.

Cherene Kruger, founder of Homes for Expats, has spent years helping international buyers through their first Dutch house purchase, and her starting point is always the same: don’t assume the process works the way it does back home.

“The biggest problem is you don’t know what you don’t know,” she says. “You’re not shopping for property on your home turf, which already makes things stressful.” In the Netherlands, that unfamiliar cast list includes two makelaars (estate agents), a bank, a mortgage adviser and a notary: roles that may not exist, or might work quite differently, elsewhere.

The estate agent isn’t on your side
The most important thing to understand, says Cherene, is who actually represents whom. “The selling makelaar represents the seller. If you appoint a buying makelaar, they are the one representing your interests and fighting in your corner.”
“I once had a client who kept saying out loud how much she was prepared to pay for a house, right in front of the selling agent,” she says.

It’s a distinction that doesn’t occur to a lot of first-time buyers, and one whose consequences Cherene has experienced herself. She once bought a new-build property that didn’t automatically come with plastered and painted walls, a paved driveway or a levelled garden with grass, because no one had properly explained what was and wasn’t included beforehand.

Don’t get caught up in overbidding
While overbidding is often a fact of life in the Dutch market, knowing how much to offer can be one of the hardest things for international buyers to navigate. The asking price doesn’t reflect market value, and simply offering more isn’t always the right decision.

Cherene also sees more buyers turning to AI for answers. “AI can be a useful research tool, but it cannot replace someone being on the ground, seeing the property, understanding what’s happening in that particular market and having actual lived experience.”

Cherene’s own approach is deliberately pragmatic: research the area, weigh market value against what a property is actually worth, and look at comparable sales, understand the market value and then decide what the property is worth to you as a buyer. “My job is to help you make the right decision and the right investment,” she says. “You’re buying a house, not a hamburger, so it’s incredibly important we get this right!” She would rather see a client lose a property than win one at a cost that leaves them in negative equity for years to come.

Get financing sorted before you fall for a house
Every offer Cherene puts together includes two standard conditions: a financing clause and a technical inspection. Both protect the buyer. If financing falls through without a financing condition, the buyer could face a penalty of 10% of the purchase price. A technical inspection condition offers protection if serious defects are uncovered.

For instance, the inspection can unearth problems like hidden mould or rotten beams that aren’t obvious during a viewing. “If there’s a major issue that is going to cost my clients a lot of money, I would rather walk away from a bad relationship than marry just for the sake of getting married.” Depending on how the technical inspection condition has been agreed, serious defects may give the buyer the opportunity to renegotiate or withdraw from the purchase.

For buyers relocating for work, getting that financial picture in order early is arguably the single most useful thing they can do. Once a client signs with Homes for Expats, Cherene advises them to register with a mortgage adviser or their bank and have their documents submitted before the serious house hunting begins. That way, they know what’s actually affordable and are in a position to move when they find the right home.

Homes for Expats sets out the buying process in more detail, but the underlying message is consistent: have the financing conversation before the house hunting starts, not after you’ve found the one.

What you see isn’t necessarily what you get
One of Cherene’s most vivid cases involved an apartment marketed as a two-bedroom, which her clients fell in love with. When she started digging into the property’s deed of division, however, the numbers didn’t add up: the apartment was around 10 square metres smaller on the deed than advertised, and that second “bedroom” up a flight of stairs was in fact a storage room.

The room wasn’t listed on the deed of division as residential space, the deed of division had never been amended to change its designated use, and the previous owner had never obtained permission to convert the storage space into liveable accommodation, either from the gemeente (local council) or from the building’s VvE (owners’ association).

Cherene is clear on the lesson: “Triple-check everything. A property’s paperwork, the deed of division, VvE permissions and permit history can tell a very different story from the one a listing suggests. And if something isn’t documented, there’s probably a reason for that.”

Dutch rules may not be what you’d expect
A recurring misconception is that owning property automatically means being free to rent it out for extra income, as it might elsewhere. In the Netherlands, that’s not necessarily the case. Your mortgage conditions, municipal rules, VvE rules and Dutch tenancy law can all affect whether and how a property may be rented.

“Most people have been taught you can generate wealth this way,” she says, “but it’s different in the Netherlands.” It’s a reminder that runs through all of Cherene’s advice: assume nothing carries over from home, however similar it looks on the surface.

Getting the keys
Cherene admits to a soft spot for first-time buyers specifically: “If I do my job well, I set the bar for every real estate transaction they’ll ever make. You’ll always remember the first home you buy. I get to be part of people’s joy, and for me that is my “why’”.

“I love helping people, and this fits so perfectly into that part of me. If I do my job right, I haven’t just helped them buy a house. I’ve been part of them buying their very first home, something they will never forget.”

For many of her clients, most of them a long way from where they grew up, the moment they get the keys is about more than the property itself. It’s the point at which the Netherlands really feels like home.

For anyone starting to think about buying, Cherene’s advice is simple: get your financial ducks in a row, and book a free chat with Homes for Expats before you start house hunting.

item.title: Amsterdam university bans laptops and mobiles from lecture hall
item.description:
Amsterdam university bans laptops and mobiles from lecture hall

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Students who have enrolled for a sociology course at the University of Amsterdam this year have been told to leave electronic devices at the door and go back to taking notes by hand.

The UvA has banned laptops, mobile phones and tablets from lectures and classes in interdisciplinary social science, on the grounds that they interefere with students’ concentration.

Senior lecturer Cyrilien Evertsen told NOS that “60% to 80% of students are doing things on digital devices during classes other than listening”, such as shopping or chatting on social media. “They’re not mentally present in the class,” she said.

Paul Kirschner, emeritus professor of educational psychology at Utrecht University, backed the stance, arguing that switching off devices and taking notes by hand makes students engage directly with the lecture material.

“Switch off all electronic devices because it’s a weapon of mass distraction,” he said.

“If you’re checking your email, you’re not following the class,” he said. “You might think that’s not so bad, but research has shown that people to your left and right get distracted and do significantly worse as a result.”

He added that handwriting forced students to select and summarise what information they take down because it is a slower process than typing.

“So you’re digesting the information, and learning is digesting,” he said.

item.title: Amsterdam man arrested over links to ShinyHunters hacking group
item.description:
Amsterdam man arrested over links to ShinyHunters hacking group

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 24-year-old man from Amsterdam has been arrested on suspicion of involvement with the hacking group ShinyHunters, which has been behind a number of large-scale attacks on Dutch businesses in the past year.

Police said on social media that he was arrested this month and will appear in court in Rotterdam on Wednesday.

Sources told broadcaster NOS that the suspect is Pepijn van der S., who was sentenced to four years in prison in 2023 for extortion, money laundering and hacking. He was released this year.

Van der S. reportedly has a background in legitimate cybersecurity, having worked for Amsterdam-based security firm Hadrian. He also carried out ethical hacking research with the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure. At the same time, he was leaking data stolen from clients and other companies, the court found in 2023.

ShinyHunters was responsible for an attack on Dutch telecoms provider Odido earlier this year, in which millions of customers had their personal data stolen. After the company refused to pay a ransom, the group posted much of the data on the dark web.

The hackers were also behind an attack on Canvas, an online learning platform used by students, after which its parent company paid a ransom to prevent further disruption.

Last week, ShinyHunters also claimed to have accessed the details of thousands of employees at the FBI, the US federal law enforcement agency. The FBI said an investigation was underway.

item.title: The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?
item.description:
Partner content

The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?

September 29, 2026

The IamExpat Fair returns to Eindhoven on Saturday October 3 for its second outing in the city, with a bigger careers section, two international centres and a new kids area.

The fair, which takes place in the Klokgebouw in Strijp-S, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, including special offers only available for attendees. You can register for free online.

“We are bringing back the large career section, expanding the number of expat centres at the fair, and growing the Family & Kids section,” says event manager Claire Leunissen.

Workshops and presentations 
The fair will also feature over 20 free workshops to help expats with job hunting, finding housing, immigration and settling advice, as well as tips on local leisure and health services, and more. The workshops have limited capacity and are filling up fast, so make sure to book seats as soon as possible — you can sign up here.

Careers and partners
The careers section includes Brainport and recruitment agency Undutchables, and offers additional advice and services for the partners of people who have moved to the region for work.

“The international community of Eindhoven can’t be underestimated,” says Claire. “Because of this small but mighty community, we are bringing the Fair back to Eindhoven to support internationals and their families looking to to settle into Dutch life as well, through career opportunities, community groups, fitness schools, Dutch classes, and more.”

Families and newcomers
New this year is a kids area, supervised by childcare provider Korein, where families can play while parents work their way round the stands.

Two international centres will be on hand for questions about registration and residency: Holland Expat Center South, based in Eindhoven, and Expat Centre Maastricht Region. Orion Immigration Law returns with a stand double the size of last year’s.

Language schools include Language Institute Regina Coeli in Vught, Una Paloma Blanca, Bart de Pau and Taalkracht, while the health and leisure exhibitors range from bike subscription service Swapfiets to Happy Bodies and Shakti Nutrition.

Every stage covered
Workshops and presentations by experts run for most of the day, covering renting, buying a house and securing a mortgage, tax, careers and schooling.

“The fair is an incredible one-stop shop for every part of life in the Netherlands,” says Claire. “International students or young professionals may initially come to the Fair looking for Dutch language classes or career opportunities, but later in life, they come to the Fair for different needs, such as preparing for retirement, buying their first home, or choosing the right daycare for their kids.”

“We are excited to bring the IamExpat Fair back to the Klokgebouw, a historic building that embodies the history of technology, innovation and immigration of Eindhoven,” says Claire.

The IamExpat Fair Eindhoven takes place in the Klokgebouw, Strijp-S on Saturday October 3 from 10am to 5pm. Entrance is free with online registration.

item.title: Amsterdam wants simpler rules to get asylum seekers working
item.description:
Amsterdam wants simpler rules to get asylum seekers working

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam is making a scheme to help asylum seekers find paid work a permanent fixture, after a pilot involving over 1,000 refugees managed to get 332 of them into jobs in just over 18 months.

The city council is also calling on the national government to make it easier for employers to hire asylum seekers, by scrapping the work permit they currently need.

“It is important that asylum seekers get the chance to work while their application is still being processed,” work and income chief Sofyan Mbarki said in a statement. “Work gives people self-esteem and an income, and it helps them integrate quickly.”

Participants were recruited at three locations: the Willinklaan refugee centre and the emergency shelters at the A&O Hostel in Zuidoost and on board the MS Galaxy, a cruise ship that is being temporarily used to house asylum seekers.

National plans
Mbarki said the results backed up last week’s advice by the socio-economic council, which said councils should be legally required to help newcomers find work that matches their skills.

He also welcomed plans by work and participation minister Thierry Aartsen (VVD) to have councils help 75,000 more people into work, but said councils would need funding from The Hague to do it.

Drop-out risk
The pilot officially ends this year but will continue for another 4 years, as set out in the city’s coalition agreement.

The evaluation, by urban research institute Platform31, found that work gave participants more financial stability and helped their language skills. Employers described them as motivated and keen to learn.

It also recommended more aftercare and job coaching in the first months, to reduce the number of people who drop out of jobs after being placed.

Amsterdam wants the work permit (tewerkstellingsvergunning) replaced with a simple obligation to notify the UWV, the system already used for displaced Ukrainians in the Netherlands.

item.title: Apartment block evacuated after fire breaks out in Apeldoorn
item.description:
Apartment block evacuated after fire breaks out in Apeldoorn

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dozens of people had to be evacuated from a block of flats in Apeldoorn after a fire broke out in the early hours of Tuesday.

Residents of 30 apartments were told to leave their homes after firefighters were called out to the complex on Wagenstraat at around 2am, where a third-floor flat was ablaze.

Two people were taken to hospital as a precaution after inhaling smoke, local newspaper De Stentor reported. Five others were checked over by paramedics at the scene.

Firefighters used a cherry-picker to reach people who were unable to leave their apartments via the fire escape.

Police believe the fire may have been started deliberately. Enquiries are ongoing.
